meta.headline: Does eating organic food make you healthier, or lower your cancer risk?
meta.seoTitle: Organic food and health: what the studies show

dek.text: Reviews of the research find no health benefit of eating organic that has been proven in people, and the large cancer cohorts disagree, in groups whose diets and habits also differ.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says the current evidence base does not allow a definitive statement on the long-term health benefits of organic dietary intake, and the AAP report says no well-powered human study directly demonstrates health benefits from an organic diet.
qualifications: question-1 carries what is not known in its unresolved callout on this claim.

assertions.text: The Million Women Study found no association for reduced cancer incidence apart from a possibly lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, while NutriNet-Santé reported a lower overall cancer hazard in its top organic quartile, and the cohorts conflict on breast cancer.
qualifications: The dek says the cohorts disagree rather than that the question is settled; question-2 gives both.

assertions.text: High organic consumers differed from low consumers in diet, activity, smoking and, in NutriNet-Santé, income and education.
qualifications: The dek names diets and habits, not wealth; question-2 says income differed less in the UK cohort.

description.text: Organic eaters look healthier in observational studies, but reviews find no proven benefit, and the cancer evidence is split and confounded.

assertions.text: The Vigar review reports significant positive outcomes from observational studies, while the evidence base does not allow a definitive statement of long-term benefit.
qualifications: question-1 carries what is not known in its unresolved callout on this claim.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says the NutriNet-Santé and Million Women findings agree on non-Hodgkin lymphoma and are in direct contrast on breast cancer.
qualifications: The description says split, not settled; question-2 gives both cohorts.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says any benefits from organic food consumption may be attributable partly to increased wholefood intake and a healthier lifestyle.
qualifications: question-2 says the socioeconomic differences were smaller in the UK cohort.

sections.name: hook
sections.heading: Organic eaters are healthier. Is the food the reason?

sentences.text: If you pay extra for organic food, you are probably paying for your health as much as for the farm.
Is that what you get, and does it reach the disease people fear most, cancer?
What follows sets out what the reviews and the large cohorts found, and where their evidence stops.

sections.name: question-1
sections.heading: Does eating organic food actually make you healthier?

sentences.text: On YouTube, Seeker puts the case plainly: "it seems to me that organic has lots of health benefits".

assertions.text: Seeker said it seems to its presenter that organic has lots of health benefits.

quote.text: it seems to me that organic has lots of health benefits
quote.speaker: Seeker

sentences.text: The Organic Trade Association's site goes further, saying organic "reduces your exposure to birth defects, obesity, diabetes, ADHD, and other health problems".

assertions.text: ota.com said eating organic reduces your exposure to birth defects, obesity, diabetes, ADHD and other health problems.

quote.text: reduces your exposure to birth defects, obesity, diabetes, ADHD, and other health problems

sentences.text: The Mayo Clinic is more cautious: "Aside from lessened contact with pesticides, proven links between health and organic food are less clear."

assertions.text: Mayo Clinic wrote that aside from lessened contact with pesticides, proven links between health and organic food are less clear.

quote.text: Aside from lessened contact with pesticides, proven links between health and organic food are less clear.
quote.speaker: Mayo Clinic

sentences.text: A systematic review of the research found that, in observational studies, people who ate more organic food had lower rates of metabolic syndrome, high BMI, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, infertility, birth defects, allergic sensitisation, ear infections and pre-eclampsia.

assertions.text: The Vigar systematic review reports significant positive outcomes from observational studies, including reduced incidence of metabolic syndrome, high BMI, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, infertility, birth defects, allergic sensitisation, otitis media and pre-eclampsia, while the evidence base does not allow a definitive statement of long-term benefit.
qualifications: s07 says these are observational studies; s08 gives the review's warning about diet and weight.

sentences.text: The same review cautions that organic eating usually travels with a healthier diet overall and less overweight and obesity, which it judges likely to influence those observational results.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says organic food consumption is often tied to healthier dietary practices and lower levels of overweight and obesity, which are likely to be influential in the results of observational research.

sentences.text: A second review saw hints of fewer childhood allergies, less adult obesity and less non-Hodgkin lymphoma among organic consumers, but judged that it cannot yet be determined whether organic food causes any of them.

assertions.text: The Mie review reports indications of lower childhood allergies, adult overweight/obesity and non-Hodgkin lymphoma in organic consumers, and says it is presently not possible to determine whether organic food plays a causal role.

sentences.text: Its authors add that people who prefer organic eat more fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes and less meat, a pattern that would by itself be expected to lower their risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

assertions.text: The Mie review says consumers who prefer organic food eat more fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes and less meat, and expects them to have a decreased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease as a consequence of these dietary patterns.

sentences.text: Trials, in which researchers change what people eat, have so far run for short periods and mostly tracked surrogate markers, with few positive results.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says clinical trial research has been short-term and measured largely surrogate markers with limited positive results.

sentences.text: The Stanford review counted 17 studies in people, of which only 3 measured clinical outcomes, and those found no significant differences in eczema, wheeze, allergic sensitisation or symptomatic Campylobacter infection.

assertions.text: The Smith-Spangler review included 17 human studies; only 3 examined clinical outcomes, finding no significant differences for allergic outcomes (eczema, wheeze, atopic sensitization) or symptomatic Campylobacter infection.
qualifications: s12 names it as one review and says how few of its human studies looked at illness.

blocks.caption: Human studies in the Stanford review, and how many of them looked at actual illness.

sentences.text: In adults, its studies of nutrients and other markers in blood, urine, breast milk and semen showed no clinically meaningful differences.

assertions.text: The Smith-Spangler review reports that studies of biomarker and nutrient levels in serum, urine, breast milk and semen in adults did not identify clinically meaningful differences.
qualifications: s13 keeps to adults and to biomarker studies in the same review.

sentences.text: A clinical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics found no well-powered human study that directly demonstrates a health benefit or protection from disease as a result of an organic diet.

assertions.text: The AAP report says there are no well-powered human studies that directly demonstrate health benefits or disease protection from consuming an organic diet.
qualifications: s14 keeps the report's own wording (well-powered, directly).

sentences.text: A meta-analysis of organic milk found it differs in composition, but its authors say virtually no studies have measured what eating organic does to health; a companion analysis of meat adds that no cohort study yet links organic meat to less eczema or other health gains.

assertions.text: The Srednicka-Tober milk meta-analysis reports significant differences in nutritionally relevant compounds and says there are virtually no studies in which impacts of organic food consumption on human health or health-related biomarkers were assessed.
The Srednicka-Tober meat meta-analysis says there are so far no cohort studies showing a link between organic meat consumption and reduced incidence of eczema and other positive health outcomes.

sentences.text: And a risk model of pesticide residues on the Dirty Dozen produce found nothing to indicate that swapping the conventional forms for organic ones would bring a measurable health benefit.

assertions.text: Winter and Katz write that their findings do not indicate that substituting organic forms of the Dirty Dozen commodities for conventional forms will lead to any measurable consumer health benefit.
qualifications: s16 calls it a risk model of pesticide residues, not a study of people.

sentences.text: What remains open is whether eating less pesticide matters: studies consistently find fewer pesticide metabolites in the urine of people on an organic diet, the evidence is insufficient to show that this turns into a meaningful health outcome, and the systematic review's authors still think it possible that lower exposure kept up over time may bring health benefits.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says pesticide excretion studies have consistently shown a reduction in urinary pesticide metabolites with an organic diet, but there is insufficient evidence that this translates into clinically meaningful health outcomes.
The Vigar review says it seems possible that ongoing reduced pesticide exposure may translate to health benefits.

sentences.text: So the benefit is unproven rather than ruled out: the trials that could test it have been short and have mostly measured markers rather than disease.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says clinical trial research has been short-term and measured largely surrogate markers, and the evidence base does not allow a definitive statement on long-term health benefits.

sentences.text: These reviews differ less in their verdict than in what they examined, from the composition of milk to pesticide risk models to outcomes in people, and none of them concludes that eating organic has been shown to cause a health benefit.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says the current evidence base does not allow a definitive statement on the long-term health benefits of organic dietary intake.
The Mie review says it is presently not possible to determine whether organic food plays a causal role in the observed health differences.
The AAP report says there are no well-powered human studies that directly demonstrate health benefits or disease protection as a result of consuming an organic diet.

sentences.text: On the evidence so far, then, no health benefit of eating organic has been shown in the people who eat it, though the reviews leave the question open.

assertions.text: The reviews find that the evidence does not allow a definitive statement on long-term health benefits of organic food, and no well-powered human study demonstrates one.

sentences.text: That brings us to the outcome where the boldest claims are made: cancer.

sections.name: question-2
sections.heading: Does eating organic food lower your risk of cancer?

sentences.text: On the ZOE channel, Tim Spector describes a study in which "the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent".

assertions.text: Tim Spector said that in one study the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent against cancer.

quote.text: the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent
quote.speaker: Tim Spector

sentences.text: Renegade Dietitian gives the reasoning behind such claims: "less pesticide equals lower risk exposure, which equals better long-term odds".

assertions.text: Renegade Dietitian said less pesticide equals lower risk exposure, which equals better long-term odds.

quote.text: less pesticide equals lower risk exposure, which equals better long-term odds
quote.speaker: Renegade Dietitian

sentences.text: F. Perry Wilson, MD, puts the doctor's question and answers it: "Should you encourage your patients to eat organic? Not on the basis of this study."

assertions.text: F. Perry Wilson, MD, said doctors should not encourage patients to eat organic on the basis of this study.

quote.text: Should you encourage your patients to eat organic? Not on the basis of this study.
quote.speaker: F. Perry Wilson, MD

sentences.text: The French NutriNet-Santé cohort tracked 68,946 adults for a mean of 4.6 years, and after adjustment for confounders, those in the top quarter of an organic food score had a hazard of cancer 25 percent below the bottom quarter's, a hazard ratio of 0.75.

assertions.text: NutriNet-Santé followed 68,946 participants for a mean of 4.6 years; after adjustment for confounders, the top quartile of organic food score had a hazard ratio of 0.75 for overall cancer against the bottom quartile, a 25 percent lower hazard.
qualifications: s26 gives the absolute difference; the unresolved callouts on gap 2 and on this claim give the confounding.

sentences.text: Expressed as an absolute risk reduction, that gap was 0.6 percent.

assertions.text: NutriNet-Santé reports an absolute risk reduction of 0.6% for the top against the bottom quartile of organic food score.
qualifications: s26 itself gives the absolute size of the relative drop in s25.

sentences.text: By cancer type, the lower risk appeared for non-Hodgkin lymphoma and postmenopausal breast cancer, with no association for the other types.

assertions.text: Among specific cancers, NutriNet-Santé found a decreased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and postmenopausal breast cancer, with no association for other types of cancer.
qualifications: s27 narrows the overall association to two cancers and none for the rest.

sentences.text: The British Million Women Study was far larger, and found that those who usually or always ate organic had no lower rate of cancer overall than those who never did.

assertions.text: In the Million Women Study, self-reported usually/always organic consumption against never was not associated with a reduction in all cancer (RR 1.03, CI 0.99-1.07).

sentences.text: Breast cancer was slightly more common in its organic group, and the only cancer that was less common was non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which the authors' conclusion qualifies as "except possibly for non-Hodgkin lymphoma".

assertions.text: In the Million Women Study, usually/always organic consumption was associated with slightly higher breast cancer (RR 1.09) and lower non-Hodgkin lymphoma (RR 0.79), and the authors concluded there was little or no decrease in cancer except possibly for non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

blocks.caption: The two large cohorts on organic food and overall cancer, side by side

cells.label: Hazard ratio, top vs bottom quarter of organic food score

rows.label: Million Women Study, UK women (2014 report)

cells.label: Relative risk, usually or always vs never eating organic

blocks.caption: The French cohort's size beside the absolute difference in cancer it found.

sentences.text: Read together, the cohorts point the same way on lymphoma and opposite ways on breast cancer.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says the NutriNet-Santé finding on non-Hodgkin lymphoma is similar to the Million Women Study's, while the finding on breast cancer is in direct contrast.
qualifications: s30 gives the signal the cohorts share beside the one where they conflict.

sentences.text: In the French cohort, a higher organic score went with being a woman, higher income or occupational status, a degree, more physical activity, more fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes, and less meat.

assertions.text: In NutriNet-Santé, higher organic food scores were associated with female sex, high occupational status or income, postsecondary education and physical activity, and with higher intake of fruits, vegetables, nuts and legumes and lower intake of processed meat, other meat and poultry.
qualifications: s32 says the socioeconomic differences were smaller in the UK cohort.

sentences.text: In the British cohort, regular organic eaters reported more strenuous exercise and were less likely to smoke or eat red and processed meat, but their socioeconomic status differed less.

assertions.text: In the Million Women Study, women who usually or always ate organic were more likely to report strenuous physical activity and less likely to smoke or eat red and processed meat, with smaller differences in socioeconomic status.
qualifications: s32 itself says the socioeconomic differences were smaller.

sentences.text: The French team reports that accounting for further dietary factors left its result unchanged, yet the systematic review notes that studies measure and adjust for diet in different ways, so an apparent benefit may owe something to wholefood diets and healthier lives rather than to organic food itself.

assertions.text: NutriNet-Santé reports that accounting for other additional dietary factors did not modify its finding on organic food score and overall cancer risk.
qualifications: The same sentence gives the systematic review's caveat; s26 gives the small absolute difference.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says diet quality has been measured and adjusted for in different ways in observational research, and that any benefits from organic food consumption may be attributable partly to increased wholefood intake and a healthier lifestyle, rather than a direct effect of organic food.
qualifications: s33 says partly, not wholly; s32 says income differed less in the UK cohort.

sentences.text: Why the cohorts split is not settled, but an analysis of US cohorts offers one reading: produce low in pesticide residues was not linked to the cancers earlier tied to organic food, which suggests those links reflect education, activity, not smoking and moderate drinking rather than less pesticide in the diet.

assertions.text: Sandoval-Insausti found that low-pesticide-residue fruit and vegetable intake was not associated with malignancies previously inversely linked to organic food, suggesting the organic-food associations might reflect high education, physical activity, no smoking and moderate alcohol consumption rather than a biological effect of lower dietary pesticide exposure.
qualifications: s34 calls it one reading and says the split is not settled; that analysis did not measure organic intake.

sentences.text: The same US authors point out that the French association, in stratified analyses, appears confined to the groups most likely to eat organic, such as women, older people and those with a family history of cancer, which raises concerns about residual and unmeasured confounding.

assertions.text: Sandoval-Insausti argue that organic food consumption is a complex behaviour that adjustment may not entirely capture, and that NutriNet-Santé's associations appear restricted in stratified analyses to subgroups more likely to consume organic foods, including women, older individuals and those with a family history of cancer, raising concerns about residual and unmeasured confounding.
qualifications: s35 reports it as the US authors' argument, not a measurement.

sentences.text: The systematic review that sets both cohorts side by side adds that self-reported organic intake has not been validated, and that the benefit seen may be partly down to diet quality rather than organic food.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says the benefit observed for organic intake may be partly due to the quality and composition of the diet rather than a direct effect of organic food consumption, and that validation of self-reported organic intake in observational studies is lacking.

sentences.text: That organic eaters live differently holds more clearly for health habits than for wealth: the British cohort found only small socioeconomic differences, and a USDA report describes organic consumers as fairly diverse in income, race and ethnicity, though price remains a barrier for some.

assertions.text: In the Million Women Study, socioeconomic differences by frequency of organic food consumption were smaller than the differences in activity, smoking and meat intake.
The USDA ERS report says organic consumers have always been fairly diverse in income, race and ethnicity, though price may be a barrier for some.

sentences.text: The question stays open: the one cancer both cohorts tie to organic eating is non-Hodgkin lymphoma, the British authors hedged even that, and the French result comes from people whose diets and lives differed from those who rarely ate organic.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says the NutriNet-Santé finding on non-Hodgkin lymphoma is similar to the Million Women Study's, which found no reduced cancer incidence except a possibly lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
In NutriNet-Santé, higher organic food scores were associated with higher income, education and physical activity and a healthier diet.

sentences.text: Taken together, the cohorts do not show that eating organic lowers cancer risk: the bigger study saw no overall drop, and the smaller saw a 0.6 percent absolute difference in a group whose diet and habits also set it apart.

assertions.text: The Million Women Study found no reduction in all cancer with organic food, and NutriNet-Santé found an absolute risk reduction of 0.6% in its top organic quartile, so organic food has not been shown to lower cancer risk.
qualifications: s39 names the small absolute difference and the lifestyle differences in the cohort that found it.

assertions.text: High organic consumers in NutriNet-Santé also differed in diet and lifestyle, which may account for part of any benefit.
qualifications: s32 says income differed less in the UK cohort.

sections.name: close
sections.heading: How to read the next claim that organic food keeps you well

sentences.text: Both answers turn on the same test: were the people in the study given organic food, or did they choose it along with the rest of how they live?
Then ask what was counted, cases of disease or a marker in blood or urine, and for how long.
And when a result comes as a percentage lower risk, look for the absolute difference beside it.
